title: TC0-03695
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (Appellant), citizen of Zimbabwe, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated January 16, 2020, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant), citizen of Zimbabwe, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated January 16, 2020, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
In reaching this decision, I have considered the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.1 BACKGROUND

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she fears returning to Zimbabwe because she fears harm at the hands of her former partner, XXXX XXXX. She also fears persecution based on her XXXX XXXX for the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard on February 25, 2019, May 15, 2019, and December 9, 2019. By a decision of January 16, 2020, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD found the determinative issue was credibility.

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its assessment of her credibility, failed to consider the country conditions documents with regard to her risk as an XXXX XXXX person, and erred in its assessment of her risk as an XXXX XXXX person. ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 ANALYSIS New evidence presented by the Appellant

According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.4

In the Appellant's Record, the Appellant provided seven pieces of new evidence:5 a. Appellant's Affidavit, dated June 30, 2020; b. Exhibit 1 - Basis of Claim (BOC) form narrative; c. Exhibit 2 - News Article: "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX," dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014; d. Exhibit 3 - News Article: "Hit man exposes Mzembi assassination plot," dated January 31, 2018; e. Exhibit 4 - Medical documents from Canada; f. Exhibit 4 - Medical document from Zimbabwe; and g. Exhibit 5 - Affidavit of Appellant's sister, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015.
Items (b), (c), (e), and (g) in the list above are rejected as new evidence because they appear in the RPD record and are therefore not new.

I have accepted item (a), the Appellant's Affidavit, into evidence as it meets the criteria outlined above. The affidavit contains information that speaks to the Appellant's risk in Zimbabwe, as a person who is XXXX XXXX, as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. As the pandemic was declared after the RPD's decision, I find that the evidence arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available at the time of the decision, and that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to provide this information to the RPD before its decision. I also find that the affidavit contains information that is new, the affidavit is sworn and therefore appears to be credible on its face, and the information in the affidavit is relevant to the appeal. The affidavit is therefore admitted as new evidence.

In my view, this appeal can be determined without deciding on the admissibility of the rest of the Appellant's new evidence. The proposed evidence does not affect the disposition, based on my findings below. Therefore, it is unnecessary for me to assess whether the submitted documents are admissible. They were not considered in the determination of this appeal. Merits of the Appeal

I find the determinative issue in this appeal is whether the Appellant faces discrimination amounting to persecution in Zimbabwe due to her XXXX XXXX status. Therefore, I have limited my analysis to this issue.

The RPD found the Appellant did not adduce sufficient evidence to establish that medical treatment would not be forthcoming to her in Zimbabwe, when she seeks it out. The RPD concluded that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in Zimbabwe, related to being denied medical treatment for XXXXor for XXXX.

The Appellant argues the RPD erred in its conclusion as it failed to recognize that societal discrimination and lack of access to healthcare can amount to a serious possibility of persecution. She also argues that the RPD erred by ignoring country condition documents that indicate XXXX XXXX persons face discrimination, including the provision of sub-standard medical treatment, widespread social discrimination, marginalization, and exclusion. The Appellant argues the RPD's assessment of her prospective risk of persecution was deficient because the RPD failed to refer to documents in the National Documentation Package (NDP) that were particularly relevant to the assessment of her forward-looking risk. The Appellant argues she would face a serious possibility of persecution in Zimbabwe on a forward-looking basis due, in part, to the lack of medical supplies as a result of the deteriorating economic conditions, the expensive cost of XXXX treatment, shame, and social stigma.
I have reviewed the record and conducted an independent assessment of the evidence. I accept, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is XXXX XXXX.6
I also find that the Appellant's arguments have merit. I am persuaded by the submissions and evidence of the Appellant with regard to the RPD's errors and her forward-facing risk in Zimbabwe.

The RPD did assess some evidence in the NDP, specifically with regard to the prevalence rate of XXXX in Zimbabwe and the sporadic shortages of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, in finding that medical treatment would be forthcoming to the Appellant. However, the RPD failed to consider the country condition documents with respect to other risks faced by persons with XXXX XXXX such as discrimination and other forms of mistreatment.

In her testimony at the RPD hearing, the Appellant explained that having XXXX is considered taboo in Zimbabwe, that others think it is a result of engaging in sexual or bad behaviour, and that those with XXXX are dejected and isolated. She testified she also feared experiencing this kind of discrimination in hospitals.7

In her affidavit, the Appellant explains that she would face discrimination in Zimbabwe due to her XXXX XXXX status. She also explains that the health sector in Zimbabwe experiences significant problems, that her health is more at risk due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and that returning to Zimbabwe will make her more vulnerable.8
Based on the above, I find the Appellant credible, on a balance of probabilities, with regard to her fears of returning to Zimbabwe as an XXXX XXXX person.
Given that I have found the Appellant and her allegations of fear on this basis credible, on a balance of probabilities, I now turn to the well-foundedness of her fears.

With regard to her forward-facing risk, there are objective reports that corroborate that XXXX treatment remains out of reach for many, there are fears of stigma and discrimination, and that in the past, the government cut off treatment for some individuals and ordered them to buy their own medication as there were too many people requiring state assistance.9

It is also reported that despite laws prohibiting discrimination against those with XXXX XXXX societal discrimination remained a problem. Discrimination was reported "in health services, education, and employment." Further, this ostracism and criticism continued despite an information campaign to destigmatize XXXX.10

It is also reported that, '90% of healthcare institutions don't have essential medicines in stock, and there have been sporadic shortages of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ... 'a monthly supply of XXXX [costs] between $XXXXand XXXX XXXX. An XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX examination, which is needed to determine whether patients are responding well to XXXX XXXX can cost up to $XXXX at a private laboratory. Most public healthcare institutions don't offer this service.' 'The medical system is in such disarray that nearly two-thirds of sick Zimbabweans do not seek out the treatment they need because they can't afford it, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economic Development.'11

The Appellant also cited a study, in which it was found that people living with XXXX 'still experience different forms of stigma and discrimination which include being gossiped about, exclusion from social, religious and family activities, verbal and physical abuse among other things. XXXX related stigma is reported to be still evident in the workplace, educational institutions, and also in the health institutions.'12
Therefore, based on the Appellant's circumstances and the objective evidence, I find her risk in Zimbabwe is objectively well-founded.

I find the objective evidence establishes that she would be at risk of persecution if returned to Zimbabwe based on the cumulative effect of discrimination and stigmatization against people living with XXXX. If returned to Zimbabwe, many of her core human rights, including re-establishment and access to medical services, will be restricted to the extent that it would amount to persecution. I find that the discrimination will affect all aspects of her life, including her ability to work, find housing, participate in community events, and access medical treatment.
Given the above, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant would be at risk of persecution if returned to Zimbabwe based on the cumulative effect of discrimination.

The objective evidence establishes that people with XXXX face discrimination in various fields of life and there is no evidence that certain areas of Zimbabwe are free from this discrimination. I therefore find that the Appellant's risk exists throughout Zimbabwe and I do not find that the Appellant has a viable Internal Flight Alternative.

I also find that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming for the Appellant in her particular circumstances. Although there are laws and programs in place to protect those with XXXX XXXX discrimination remains a problem. Further, part of what forms the Appellant's risk is created by the government itself; that being her access to medication and adequate healthcare. I therefore find that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming for the Appellant.

Based on all of the above, and having conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, and based on the past experiences of the Appellant and the country condition evidence, I find that the Appellant would experience discrimination which would cumulatively lead to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature that would amount to persecution should she return to Zimbabwe. I therefore find that there is a serious possibility that the Appellant would suffer persecution should she return to Zimbabwe because of her XXXX XXXX status. For this reason, I grant the appeal.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. (signed) Inderpreet K. Singh I.
